t: The Secretary of the Army may establish or develop Army installations and facilities by proceeding with construction made necessary by changes in Army missions and responsibilities which have been occasioned by: (a) unforeseen security considerations, (b) new weapons developments, (c) new and unforeseen research and development requirements, or (d) improved production schedules, if the Secretary of Defense determines that deferral of such construction for inclusion in the next Military Construction Authorization Act would be inconsistent with interests of national security, and in connection therewith to acquire, construct, convert, rehabilitate. or install permanent or temporary public works, including land acquisition, site preparation, appurtenances, utilities, and equipment, in the total amount of $10,000,000: Provided, That the Secretary of the Army, or his designee, shall notify the Committees on Armed Services of the Senate and House of Representatives, immediately upon reaching a final decision to implement, of the cost of construction of any public work undertaken under this section, including those real estate actions pertaining thereto. This authorization will expire as of September 30, 1969, except for those public works projects concerning which the Committees on Armed Services of the Senate and House of Representatives have been notified pursuant to this section prior to that date.

fable.w: The tempting reading treats the notification requirement as participation, but the notice goes only to congressional committees, which are inside the federal government, and it comes after the decision is already final. The only other actors are the Secretary of the Army and the Secretary of Defense, so any coordination is intra-governmental. No state, local, expert, or public party is consulted or given a right to object or sue.
fable.s: shall notify the Committees on Armed Services of the Senate and House of Representatives, immediately upon reaching a final decision to implement

opus.w: The only procedure here is a notice to congressional committees, plus a determination by the Secretary of Defense. Both stay entirely inside the federal government. Reports to or notices of Congress are an explicit trap: they look procedural but do not bring any outside party into the decision. No outside party is consulted or given a right to object, so this is not participation.
opus.s: Provided, That the Secretary of the Army, or his designee, shall notify the Committees on Armed Services of the Senate and House of Representatives, immediately upon reaching a final decision to implement, of the cost of construction of any public work undertaken under this section
opus.b: **Step 1.** The tempting reading is "Yes," because the Secretary of the Army must formally notify the Armed Services Committees before construction goes ahead, which sounds like a procedural check on a federal decision. That reading fails the definition. Congress and its committees are inside the federal government, and the only other actor, the Secretary of Defense making the national-security determination, is also federal. No state, tribe, expert, company or member of the public is consulted, and there is no hearing, comment period, rulemaking or right to sue.

qwen_chat.w: The section requires the Secretary of the Army to notify the Committees on Armed Services of the Senate and House of Representatives. According to the definition, Congress and its committees are inside the federal government. Notification to internal government bodies does not constitute participation with outside parties.
qwen_chat.s: Provided, That the Secretary of the Army, or his designee, shall notify the Committees on Armed Services of the Senate and House of Representatives, immediately upon reaching a final decision to implement, of the cost of construction of any public work undertaken under this section
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that notifying the Committees on Armed Services constitutes "participation" because it involves informing an external body before or during a decision. However, the definition explicitly states that "Congress, its committees and members... are all INSIDE the federal government." Therefore, reporting to Congress is intra-governmental communication, not participation with outside parties.
